summary: Describes a workflow for remote attestation of the integrity of firmware and software on network devices that contain a Trusted Platform Module or an equivalent. It is informational and sets the operational context for YANG work such as RFC 9684.

eli5.summary: A network device carries a tamper-proof notebook of what it has loaded. This explains how someone far away can read that notebook to check the device has not been secretly changed.

questions: how does remote attestation with a tpm work
what is a pcr in a tpm
subtitle: How a network operator can check from afar that a router or switch booted the software it was supposed to, using its TPM.

tldr.problem: Operators need confidence that fielded routers, switches and firewalls are authentic and launched authorized, untampered software, but a compromised device may lie about its own state (the Lying Endpoint problem).
tldr.mechanism: Each boot stage measures the next and extends the hash into a TPM. A remote Verifier sends a fresh nonce, gets back a TPM-signed Quote plus an event log, checks the device identity, and compares the results to signed Reference Values.
tldr.outcome: It gives vendors and operators a common, interoperable workflow built on existing standards, and sets the context for the CHARRA YANG model in RFC 9684.

today: RFC 9683 is an Informational document that has not been obsoleted or updated. It sets the operational context for the YANG data model in RFC 9684.

sections.title: The Remote Integrity Verification Problem
sections.content:
A generic remote attestation architecture already exists in RFC 9334, but the RFC says it does not give network equipment vendors and operators enough guidance to build interoperable devices. This document fills that gap for routers, switches and firewalls that contain a Trusted Platform Module (TPM) or an equivalent cryptoprocessor.

The goals are provable device identity, a software inventory with evidence it has not been altered without authorization, and verifiability that the software the administrator authorized is what actually launched. RIV must handle the Lying Endpoint problem, where malicious software hides its own compromise, and it should work out of the box with few provisioning steps.

Scope is limited. RIV is for non-privacy-preserving uses such as networking, assumes protocols like YANG and NETCONF, and mandates a TPM or compatible cryptoprocessor. Continuous run-time attestation, multi-vendor embedded systems, sleep modes, and virtualization and containers are out of scope.
sections.eli5: If a toy robot could lie about whether someone had tampered with it, you could not just ask it. So RIV uses a locked notebook inside the robot that it cannot fake.

sections.title: How the Boot Measurements Work
sections.content:
Attestation has two phases. In the Boot Phase, each software object is measured by the Attester: its identity, hash and version are recorded in a log, and the hash is extended into the TPM so the log entries can be validated. Each stage of the system measures the next one, and extends its measurement into the TPM before launching it, following the layered chain-of-trust model of Measured Boot.

In the Verification Phase, a separate Verifier retrieves the logs and the digests held in the TPM, signed by an attestation private key that the TPM never releases. The Verifier checks the identity in the certificate, rebuilds the digests by accumulating the hashes in the log, compares them with the signed TPM values, and then compares the logged digests with Reference Values.

Measurements go into Platform Configuration Registers (PCRs). Assignment is a manufacturer policy choice covering code, configuration and credentials. By convention most PCRs come in pairs, with the even-numbered one measuring code and the odd-numbered one measuring the associated data and configuration. PCR[0] is critical because the first measurement into it is taken by the Root of Trust for Measurement, which by definition cannot be verified by measurement.
sections.eli5: Each step of waking up writes what it just did into the locked notebook before handing over to the next step. Later, a checker reads the notebook and compares it with the list of what should be there.

sections.title: Identity and Attestation Keys
sections.content:
RIV relies on two credentials. The first is an identity key pair and certificate based on the IEEE 802.1AR DevID, signed by the device manufacturer, which here must include the device serial number. The second is an Attestation Key (AK) pair and certificate used to sign the Quote that reports software configuration. Both private keys MUST be protected by the TPM, and the two keys are likely to be different.

The AK certificate should carry the same unique device identification as the DevID certificate (same subject and subjectAltName, if present). If they do not match, or are signed by different authorities, the Verifier may be seeing an Asokan-style person-in-the-middle attack.

Devices that expect to use Secure Zero Touch Provisioning (RFC 8572) MUST ship with pre-provisioned keys, the Initial DevID (IDevID) and Initial AK (IAK), both certified by the Endorser, typically the manufacturer. Owners can add their own LDevID and Local Attestation Keys (LAK) instead.
sections.eli5: The device has two special keys: one is like its name tag, and one is like a stamp that only the notebook uses. Both are made inside the device so no one can copy them.

sections.title: The Challenge-Response Exchange
sections.content:
A Verifier, often a network management station, first needs Reference Values, delivered in signed Reference Integrity Manifests (RIMs), which are expressed as SWID or CoSWID tags. It then asks the Attester for evidence.

The Verifier generates a unique random nonce and requests one or more PCRs, as specified in RFC 9684. TPM 1.2 and TPM 2.0 allow nonces as large as the digest size, 20 or 32 bytes. The Attester returns a Quote, the requested PCR values plus the nonce signed by the AK, together with the event log. Evidence can be retrieved with NETCONF or RESTCONF over a secure tunnel.

The Verifier SHOULD NOT trust the device if the Quote signature is wrong, the nonce does not match, the signed PCR values do not match the log entries, the important log entries do not match known good values, the log fails the Appraisal Policy for Evidence, or the Evidence is staler than the policy's freshness threshold. Logs must be in the TCG UEFI event log format or the Canonical Event Log Format. The Verifier MUST have an Appraisal Policy for Evidence, but its format is not specified.

RIV can also run peer to peer, where two routers each challenge the other. In that case devices carry their own signed RIMs and appraisal policies.
sections.eli5: The checker shouts a brand-new secret word and asks the device to read its notebook back with that word written in. Because the word is new, the device cannot reuse an old, clean-looking page.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC lists four risks: compromised keys, a counterfeit device impersonating a real one, person-in-the-middle attacks where a compromised device relays a quote from an authentic one, and replay attacks. Keys are generated inside the TPM and never exposed. The DevID validates the TLS or SSH session so that it ends on the intended device, and a separate AK signs quotes so that a general-purpose identity key cannot be used to forge one. The fresh nonce in each Quote defeats replay.

Because quotes are signed inside the TPM, any later change, even reformatting, is detected. Implementations MUST preserve the TPM signing so that tampering anywhere along the path can be detected.

Other dependencies include a trustworthy first measurement by the RTM, physical defense of the device (a stolen TPM inserted into a counterfeit device could look authentic), and scrutiny of supply chains for Reference Values. TPM 1.2 only uses SHA-1, which is susceptible to collision attack, so RIV implementations SHOULD use TPM 2.0, which produces quotes with SHA-256. On privacy, attestation data is unlikely to reveal user information, but administrators may want to keep it confidential because software versions could help attackers.
sections.eli5: The locks and notebook are built inside the device so a sneaky copy cannot fake them. The checker still has to make sure the device itself was not swapped for an impostor.
